title: The Lesson I Learned From Joshua's Courage
paragraphs:
The Lesson I Learned From Joshua's Courage
When Fear Screamed the Loudest, Faith Refused to Back Down
There are moments in life when fear does not whisper.
It screams.
It echoes through your thoughts at midnight.
It sits beside your bed when everyone else is asleep.
It follows you into doctor's offices, courtrooms, funerals, broken relationships, financial crises, unanswered prayers, and seasons where God feels silent.
Fear has a voice.
But so does God.
And one of the greatest lessons I have ever learned came from a man who stood between those two voices and chose to listen to the right one.
His name was Joshua.
Most people remember Joshua as a fearless warrior.
Scripture paints a different picture.
Joshua was not courageous because he felt no fear.
Joshua was courageous because he obeyed God despite it.
That distinction changes everything.

When Moses died, Israel lost the leader they had followed for decades. The nation stood at the edge of the Promised Land, but standing between them and God's promise was the raging Jordan River, fortified cities, giant armies, and generations of uncertainty.
The future looked overwhelming.
And God knew exactly what Joshua was feeling.
That is why one of the most repeated commands in the opening chapter of Joshua is not "attack."
It is not "fight."
It is not even "lead."
It is this:
"Be strong and courageous."
In Hebrew, the phrase is:
חֲזַק וֶאֱמָץ (Chazaq Ve'ematz)
"Be strong and courageous."
The word חֲזַק (Chazaq) means to strengthen, prevail, become firm, or take hold.
The word אֱמָץ (Amatz) means to be bold, determined, steadfast, and resolute.
God was not commanding Joshua to manufacture courage.
God was commanding Joshua to hold tightly to Him.
Because biblical courage is not confidence in yourself.
Biblical courage is confidence in God.
The Lord tells Joshua:
"Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go." (Joshua 1:9)
The Hebrew phrase translated "do not be frightened" carries the idea of being shattered internally by fear.
God was not ignoring Joshua's emotions.
He was addressing them directly.
Because God knew what Joshua needed most was not a better strategy.
He needed God's presence.
That lesson has followed me through every difficult season of my life.
I used to think courage meant having certainty.
I thought courageous people never doubted.
Never struggled.
Never questioned.
Never cried.
Never wrestled.
Then life happened.
I discovered that courage often looks like trembling hands that still obey God.
It looks like praying while your heart is breaking.
It looks like moving forward while tears fill your eyes.
It looks like trusting when you do not understand.
Joshua eventually stood before Jericho, one of the most intimidating cities in the ancient world.
Its walls represented impossibility.
Humanly speaking, Israel had no chance.
No siege equipment.
No military superiority.
No logical explanation for victory.
Yet God gave Joshua instructions that sounded absurd.
Walk around the city.
Keep walking.
Trust Me.
Can you imagine how ridiculous that must have sounded?
But Joshua obeyed.
And the walls fell.
Not because Joshua was powerful.
Because God was faithful.
There is a profound truth hidden in that story.
The greatest obstacles in our lives are often not the walls around us.
They are the fears within us.
The battle is rarely external first.
It is internal.
The enemy knows that if fear can control your thoughts, it can influence your choices.
But God's Word continually calls believers to something greater.
In the Greek New Testament, Paul writes:
The word translated fear is:
δειλία (deilia)
It describes cowardice, timidity, shrinking back.
God does not call His children to retreat from His calling.
He calls them to trust Him in it.
This does not mean Christians never struggle with anxiety.
It means fear is no longer our master.
Jesus is.
And perhaps that is why Joshua's story feels so personal.
Because every one of us eventually stands before a Jordan River.
Every one of us eventually faces a Jericho.
Every one of us eventually encounters a situation where our strength is not enough.
That is where faith begins.
Not when we feel capable.
But when we realize we are not.
The greatest act of courage in history was not performed by Joshua.
It was performed by Jesus Christ.
In the Garden of Gethsemane, knowing the suffering that awaited Him, Jesus prayed:
"Not my will, but yours, be done."
The Greek text records:
οὐ τὸ θέλημά μου ἀλλὰ τὸ σὸν γινέσθω
"Not my will, but Yours be done."
That is courage.
Perfect obedience in the face of unimaginable suffering.
The cross looked like defeat.
It looked like scandal.
It looked like failure.
It looked like the end.
Yet three days later the empty tomb revealed heaven's greatest truth.
God specializes in rewriting stories.
What looked like scandal became grace.
What looked like death became life.
What looked like defeat became victory.
That is why Joshua's courage ultimately points beyond Joshua.
It points to Jesus.
Joshua's Hebrew name is יְהוֹשֻׁעַ (Yehoshua) meaning:
"Yahweh saves."
The Greek form of that name is:
Ἰησοῦς (Iēsous)
Jesus.
The greater Joshua.
The One who does not merely lead people into an earthly promised land but into eternal life.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a burden nobody else sees.
Maybe fear has been dictating your decisions.
Maybe disappointment has weakened your faith.
Maybe shame has convinced you that your story is over.
But the Gospel declares something different.
Your story is not finished.
The same God who stood beside Joshua stands beside His people today.
The same God who brought down Jericho still works miracles.
The same Savior who walked out of the tomb still transforms lives.
And the same grace that redeemed scandal still redeems sinners.
If Joshua's story teaches us anything, it is this:
Courage is not the absence of fear.
Courage is choosing obedience because God is greater than what frightens you.
So whatever wall stands before you today, do not focus on the size of the obstacle.
Focus on the size of your God.
Because faith does not deny reality.
Faith remembers that God is bigger than reality's greatest challenges.
And maybe that is exactly what your heart needed to hear today.
You never know how God might use a simple share to change a life.
What wall are you facing today?
Your testimony may encourage someone who feels alone.
Because one shared testimony can become someone's answered prayer.
Because one act of courage can change an entire generation.
Because one surrendered life can become a living testimony of grace.
And because the God who rewrote Joshua's story is still rewriting stories today.
The wall is not the end of your story. It may be the place where God is about to reveal His power.
